When readers need more than `~~GT.opt_interactive()` gives them (see
[Making Tables Interactive](24-interactive-tables.qmd)), make the table a `GTI` table. Here, the
`Make` column gets a list of its values to choose from and `HP` a range, the table is first shown
with the most powerful cars at the top, and readers can download the rows they've filtered as CSV.

```{python}
import polars as pl
from great_tables import GTI, data

gtcars_pl = data.pl.gtcars.select(["mfr", "model", "year", "hp", "trq", "msrp"])

(
    GTI(gtcars_pl)
    .tab_header(title="GT Cars: as a GTI table")
    .cols_label(mfr="Make", model="Model", year="Year", hp="HP", trq="Torque", msrp="MSRP")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["year", "hp", "trq"], use_seps=False)
    .fmt_currency(columns="msrp")
    .i_cols_filter(columns="mfr", type="facet")
    .i_cols_filter(columns="hp")
    .i_view(sort="-hp")
    .i_export("csv")
)
```

A table you've already made with `GT()`, including one with `opt_interactive()`, becomes a `GTI`
table with `GTI.from_gt()`, keeping what `opt_interactive()` set. So does one started from a
**Polars** DataFrame's `.style` property, which makes a `GT` table, and the `i_` methods follow:

```{python}
gt_tbl = (
    gtcars_pl.style
    .cols_label(mfr="Make", model="Model", year="Year", hp="HP", trq="Torque", msrp="MSRP")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["year", "hp", "trq"], use_seps=False)
    .fmt_currency(columns="msrp")
)

GTI.from_gt(gt_tbl).i_cols_filter(columns="mfr", type="facet")
```

Each of the `i_` methods has examples on its reference page (e.g., `~~GTI.i_cols_filter()`), and
the [API Reference](/reference/index.qmd#interactive-table-controls) has them all.

## The parts of a `GTI` table

A `GTI` table is the table GT made, with a few parts added around it. Here they are in teal, on a
table that's filtered by `mfr`, sorted by `hp` and scrolls within a set height:

![A GTI table with its parts labelled. The table GT made (its column labels and body) is in gray; the parts GTI adds are in teal: the status line, column controls, column profiles, row numbers, height handle, filter tokens, and the control bar with its search, keyboard shortcuts, page controls and counter, filters as text, panels, and undo and redo.](../assets/gti_parts_of_a_table.light.svg){.lightbox width="100%"}

From the top:

- The **status line**, just above the table, says what the data is and how much of it is shown
  ("Polars DataFrame · 12 of 47 rows × 4 columns"). It's there with `~~GTI.i_inspect()` (and in an
  explorer). In a table made with `opt_interactive(use_search=True)`, the search box is here too.
- The **column controls**, under each column label: the column's dtype (with `i_inspect()`), its
  sort arrows (with `~~GTI.i_sorting()`, on by default), and its filter button (with
  `~~GTI.i_cols_filter()`).
- The **column profiles**, under the labels of the columns `~~GTI.i_cols_profile()` chose: a small
  plot of how their values are spread.
- The **row numbers**, at the start of each row (with `i_inspect()`), which stay with the rows as
  they're sorted and filtered. A DataFrame's rows are numbered from 0, as its index is, and a
  DuckDB relation's or an Ibis table's from 1, as a database numbers them; `row_start=` in
  `i_inspect()` sets either one.
- The **height handle**, at the foot of a body that scrolls (with `~~GTI.i_scroll()`), dragged for
  a taller or shorter body.
- The **filter tokens**, one for each filter the rows are filtered by, which say what it keeps; a
  token's ✕ removes its filter.
- The **control bar**, just below the table, which brings together what readers can do with the
  table as a whole. From its left, it has:
  - the **search** (with `~~GTI.i_search()`, on by default) and the table's **keyboard
    shortcuts**
  - the **page controls**, around the **page counter** ("1 / 2"), which can be clicked to type a
    page to go to
  - the **filters as text** button (`{ }`, in a table with filters), which opens the filters as a
    query to edit, in the form `~~GTI.i_view()` takes them (with `filter=`)
  - the buttons that open the table's **panels**: its columns, grouping its rows and exporting them
    (when the table has these), and its info
  - **undo and redo** (with `~~GTI.i_view_state()`), and a **Reset** button once the view has
    changed

A table made with `opt_interactive()` has a **pager** below it instead of the control bar: its page
buttons, and the number of rows shown.

The status line and the control bar are close to the table, and the space that GT (or the page)
leaves around the table is kept past them, so that they read as part of it rather than of the text
around it.

A table names its own parts too: press `?` with the table focused (click in it first), or use
**Name the table's parts** in its info panel, and each part it has is outlined, with its name beside
it. `?` again, Escape, or a click outside the table puts the names away.

For a page that shows readers the parts, as this one does, `~~GTI.i_display()` with `parts=True`
names them from the start, and for good. Here's the table above, live: it works as ever under the
names, which follow its parts as you sort, filter, page or scroll it.

```{python}
(
    GTI(gtcars_pl, id="gtcars-parts")
    .cols_label(mfr="Make", model="Model", year="Year", hp="HP", trq="Torque", msrp="MSRP")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["year", "hp", "trq"], use_seps=False)
    .fmt_currency(columns="msrp")
    .i_inspect()
    .i_cols_filter(columns="mfr", type="facet")
    .i_cols_profile(columns="hp")
    .i_view(filter='mfr in ("Ferrari", "Lamborghini")', sort="-hp")
    .i_view_state()
    .i_scroll(260)
    .i_display(parts=True)
)
```

## Scrolling in place

With `~~GTI.i_scroll()`, the table takes up no more than a set height, and its body scrolls within
it. The table's header and column labels stay in view, each group's heading sticks below them while
its rows go by, and the grand summary rows at the bottom stick to the bottom. Footnotes and source
notes scroll with the body. Here are all 47 cars, with pagination off, in a body 400 pixels high.

```{python}
from great_tables import vals

gtcars_grouped = data.pl.gtcars.select(["ctry_origin", "mfr", "model", "year", "hp", "trq"])

(
    GTI(gtcars_grouped, rowname_col="model", groupname_col="ctry_origin")
    .tab_header(title="GT Cars: scrolling in place")
    .cols_label(mfr="Make", year="Year", hp="HP", trq="Torque")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["year", "hp", "trq"], use_seps=False)
    .grand_summary_rows(fns={"Average": pl.col("hp", "trq").mean()}, fmt=vals.fmt_integer)
    .i_pagination(False)
    .i_scroll(400)
)
```

Drag the height handle at the foot of the body down or up for a taller or shorter one, from a row's
height to all of the rows; a double click on it puts the set height back. The height can be a number
of pixels, or a CSS length such as `"60vh"`. Pagination and scrolling go together too: with both,
each page scrolls within the height.

## Wide tables

A table wider than its container scrolls sideways, with its stub (and the row group column, if row
groups are shown as one) staying in view on the left. A **Scroll for more →** hint and a shade at
the edge say there's more to the right, and the table's title, footnotes and source notes stay in
view as it scrolls. Here's every column of the cars, with each cell's text on one line (with
`~~GTI.i_display()`), which is more than this page has room for; scroll it with a trackpad, with
Shift and the mouse wheel, or by dragging the scrollbar.

```{python}
gtcars_wide = (
    GTI(data.pl.gtcars, rowname_col="model")
    .tab_header(title="GT Cars: every column")
    .tab_source_note("Source: the gtcars dataset.")
    .cols_label(
        mfr="Make", year="Year", trim="Trim", bdy_style="Body Style", hp="HP", hp_rpm="HP RPM",
        trq="Torque", trq_rpm="Torque RPM", mpg_c="MPG City", mpg_h="MPG Highway",
        drivetrain="Drivetrain", trsmn="Transmission", ctry_origin="Country", msrp="MSRP"
    )
    .fmt_integer(
        columns=["year", "hp", "hp_rpm", "trq", "trq_rpm", "mpg_c", "mpg_h"], use_seps=False
    )
    .fmt_currency(columns="msrp", decimals=0)
    .i_display(wrap=False)
)

gtcars_wide
```

Scrolling is one of three ways `~~GTI.i_responsive()` fits a table to a narrow container. A table
can also be stacked, each row becoming a card with each column's label next to its value, or it can
drop columns until it fits (those `~~GTI.i_cols_priority()` ranks lowest first), with a button on
each row that shows the columns dropped from it. By default, a table drops columns if any have a
priority; otherwise it's stacked in a container under 420 pixels wide if it shows no more than six
columns, and scrolls if it shows more.

## Pinned columns

With `~~GTI.i_cols_pin()`, more columns stay in view as a wide table scrolls: pinned to the left,
after the stub, or to the right. Here's the table above, with each car's make staying by its name,
and its price at the other side.

```{python}
(
    gtcars_wide
    .tab_header(title="GT Cars: with pinned columns")
    .i_cols_pin(columns="mfr")
    .i_cols_pin(columns="msrp", side="right")
)
```

Pinned columns have to be next to their side of the table, with only other pinned columns between
them and it (as `mfr` is next to the stub, and `msrp` is the last column), so a column further in is
moved there first, with `~~GT.cols_move_to_start()` or `~~GT.cols_move_to_end()`. Pinned columns
can't take up more than half of the table's container; in a narrower one, only the stub stays
pinned, until the container is wide enough again. The left is the stub's side, so in a page written
right to left, the columns pinned to the "left" are on the right, by the stub.

## Summary rows

A `GTI` table keeps the summary rows that `~~GT.summary_rows()` and `~~GT.grand_summary_rows()` add
(see [Summary Rows](06-summary-rows.qmd)). The rows are sorted within their groups, and each
group's summary rows stay with it: those at its bottom are on the page where the group ends (and
those at its top, on the page where it starts). The grand summary rows are on every page. Here, the
most powerful cars of each country come first; page through to see each country's averages, and the
averages and highest values of all the cars under every page.

```{python}
(
    GTI(gtcars_grouped, rowname_col="model", groupname_col="ctry_origin")
    .tab_header(title="GT Cars: with summary rows")
    .cols_label(mfr="Make", year="Year", hp="HP", trq="Torque")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["year", "hp", "trq"], use_seps=False)
    .summary_rows(fns={"Average": pl.col("hp", "trq").mean()}, fmt=vals.fmt_integer)
    .grand_summary_rows(
        fns={"Average": pl.col("hp", "trq").mean(), "Highest": pl.col("hp", "trq").max()},
        fmt=vals.fmt_integer,
    )
    .i_cols_filter(columns="mfr", type="facet")
    .i_view(sort="-hp")
)
```

The summary rows' values are those found in Python, from all of the data: they don't change as
readers search or filter the rows. (Choose a make in the `Make` filter, and its country's averages
are still those of all of its cars.) A group with no rows left is hidden, with its heading and
summary rows.

## Footnotes and source notes

A table's footnotes and source notes are in its footer, as in a `GT` table, and the footnote marks
stay with their cells as the rows are sorted, filtered and paged. Here, a footnote on the `HP`
label says what it is, and another marks the cars of over 700 hp; sort by `HP` to bring them to the
top.

```{python}
from great_tables import loc

(
    GTI(gtcars_pl)
    .tab_header(title="GT Cars: with footnotes and a source note")
    .cols_label(mfr="Make", model="Model", year="Year", hp="HP", trq="Torque", msrp="MSRP")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["year", "hp", "trq"], use_seps=False)
    .fmt_currency(columns="msrp")
    .tab_footnote("Horsepower, at the engine's peak.", locations=loc.column_labels(columns="hp"))
    .tab_footnote("Over 700 hp.", locations=loc.body(columns="hp", rows=pl.col("hp") > 700))
    .tab_source_note("Source: the gtcars dataset.")
)
```

The marks are numbered as the table was first made, so a sorted table can have them out of order.
The search doesn't match them, and exports leave them out. A table of a lazy frame (a Polars
LazyFrame, a DuckDB relation or an Ibis table), whose rows are collected as they're shown, can have
footnotes on its title, column labels and the rest, but not on its body or stub.

## Row details

With `~~GTI.i_row_details()`, each row can have more to show under it, when the reader asks for it.
A function makes a row's details from its values (including those of columns the table hides): as
text, with `md()` or `html()`, or as a `GT` table of their own. Here, each car has a few lines about
its engine. Click the arrow by a car's name to show them, or use **Expand all** in the table's info
panel to show every car's.

```{python}
from great_tables import md


def engine(row):
    economy = (
        "" if row["mpg_c"] is None else f" It gets {row['mpg_c']:.0f} mpg in the city, "
        f"and {row['mpg_h']:.0f} on the highway."
    )
    return md(
        f"The **{row['trim']}** ({row['bdy_style']}, {row['drivetrain'].upper()}) makes "
        f"{row['hp']:.0f} hp at {row['hp_rpm']:,.0f} rpm, and {row['trq']:.0f} lb-ft of torque."
        f"{economy}"
    )


(
    GTI(data.pl.gtcars, rowname_col="model")
    .tab_header(title="GT Cars: with row details")
    .cols_hide(
        columns=["trim", "bdy_style", "hp_rpm", "trq_rpm", "mpg_c", "mpg_h", "drivetrain", "trsmn"]
    )
    .cols_label(mfr="Make", year="Year", hp="HP", trq="Torque", ctry_origin="Country", msrp="MSRP")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["year", "hp", "trq"], use_seps=False)
    .fmt_currency(columns="msrp", decimals=0)
    .i_row_details(engine)
)
```

The details are in the table's HTML, made as it's rendered, but aren't searched, filtered or
exported (and each `GT` table in them brings its own CSS, so many of them make a larger page). A
column can hold them instead, with each row's details: `i_row_details()` takes its name, and the
column is then left out of the table.

## Column profiles

With `~~GTI.i_cols_profile()`, columns get a small plot under their labels of how their values are
spread: a histogram of numbers and dates, and bars for the most common values of the others, each
with the share of rows that have a missing value. The plots follow the rows a search or filter
keeps, so they show at a glance what's left. Here, choose a few makes in the `Make` filter and watch
the horsepower and prices narrow; point at a bar to see its values and its number of rows.

```{python}
(
    GTI(gtcars_pl)
    .tab_header(title="GT Cars: with column profiles")
    .cols_label(mfr="Make", model="Model", year="Year", hp="HP", trq="Torque", msrp="MSRP")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["year", "hp", "trq"], use_seps=False)
    .fmt_currency(columns="msrp", decimals=0)
    .i_cols_filter(columns="mfr", type="facet")
    .i_cols_profile(columns=["mfr", "year", "hp", "msrp"])
)
```

A profile's bars span the whole column, not just the rows that are left, so that they stay put as
the reader filters (only their heights change). They aren't shown when the table is stacked as
cards in a narrow container.

## Colors from the rows kept

With `data_color="recompute"` in `~~GTI.i_cols_controls()`, a column's colors from `data_color()`
are made again from the rows a search or filter keeps, as `data_color()` would make them from those
rows alone, so that the whole palette is spread over them. Here, choose a make or two in the `Make`
filter: its most powerful car takes the darkest orange, and its most expensive the darkest blue,
however they compare to the rest of the cars. Show every row again and the first colors come back.

```{python}
(
    GTI(gtcars_pl)
    .tab_header(title="GT Cars: colors from the rows kept")
    .cols_label(mfr="Make", model="Model", year="Year", hp="HP", trq="Torque", msrp="MSRP")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["year", "hp", "trq"], use_seps=False)
    .fmt_currency(columns="msrp", decimals=0)
    .data_color(columns="hp", palette=["#fff7ec", "#ef6c00"])
    .data_color(columns="msrp", palette="Blues")
    .i_cols_filter(columns="mfr", type="facet")
    .i_cols_controls(columns=["hp", "msrp"], data_color="recompute")
)
```

Sorting the rows or turning the page doesn't change the colors. Only colors that depend on the
rows can be made again: those `data_color()` made down a column from the values it found there (not
with `domain=`, nor from an ordered categorical's levels), and without `fn=`. A cell that a later
style colors keeps that style's colors.

## Grouping rows

With `groupable=True` in `~~GTI.i_cols_controls()`, readers can group the rows by any of the chosen
columns, from the **Group rows** button in the table's control bar. Each group is under a heading
with its value and its number of rows (of those a search or filter keeps), the groups in the order
of their values (or the other way around, when the column is sorted descending) with any missing
values last. The rows are sorted within their groups, and a group running over pages has its heading
on each one. Here, the cars start grouped by their country of origin, the most powerful first in
each; group them by make instead, or by none.

```{python}
by_country = data.pl.gtcars.select(["mfr", "model", "ctry_origin", "year", "hp", "msrp"])

(
    GTI(by_country)
    .tab_header(title="GT Cars: grouped by country")
    .cols_label(mfr="Make", model="Model", ctry_origin="Country", year="Year", hp="HP", msrp="MSRP")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["year", "hp"], use_seps=False)
    .fmt_currency(columns="msrp", decimals=0)
    .i_cols_controls(columns=["mfr", "ctry_origin"], groupable=True)
    .i_view(sort="-hp", group_by="ctry_origin")
)
```

The column the rows are grouped by is part of the table's view, which `~~GTI.i_view()` starts the
table with (`group_by=`) and `~~GTI.i_view_state()` can keep. This grouping is the reader's: a
table with row groups of its own (from `groupname_col=`) or with summary rows can't have columns
to group by.

## Linked tables

With `~~GTI.i_link()`, tables on the same page work together: tables with the same group name are
linked by a column they each have, so that the rows a reader selects in one filter the others to the
rows with the same values. Here, select a make or two in the first table, and the second shows only
their cars; clear the selection to show them all again.

```{python}
makes = (
    gtcars_pl.group_by("mfr")
    .agg(pl.len().alias("models"), pl.col("hp").max().alias("top_hp"))
    .sort(pl.col("mfr").str.to_lowercase())
)

(
    GTI(makes, rowname_col="mfr")
    .tab_header(title="Makes")
    .cols_label(mfr="Make", models="Models", top_hp="Top HP")
    .fmt_integer(columns="top_hp", use_seps=False)
    .i_selection("multiple")
    .i_pagination(page_size=5)
    .i_link("gtcars", on="mfr")
)
```

```{python}
(
    GTI(gtcars_pl.select(["mfr", "model", "year", "hp", "msrp"]), rowname_col="model")
    .tab_header(title="Cars")
    .cols_label(mfr="Make", year="Year", hp="HP", msrp="MSRP")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["year", "hp"], use_seps=False)
    .fmt_currency(columns="msrp", decimals=0)
    .i_link("gtcars", on="mfr")
)
```

A filtered table says what it's filtered by with a token in its control bar ("Selected in Makes:
Ferrari, Lamborghini"), which goes to the selection, and whose ✕ shows every row again (until the
selection changes); its info panel says so too. The filter is on top of the table's own search and
filters, but isn't part of its view, so it isn't kept by `~~GTI.i_view_state()`. The tables link in
the browser, with no server, so this works in a Quarto document or an HTML page, and in a notebook
whose cells' outputs share a page (in Jupyter, but not in Colab, which shows each cell's output in a
frame of its own).

## An explorer for looking through data

`GTI(df, preset="explorer")` starts a table set up for looking through a DataFrame rather than
presenting it:

- every column can be filtered, has a profile, and can be hidden and moved
- the rows are compact, each one line high (their text doesn't wrap), with the column labels and
  the values in a monospaced font
- the rows can be downloaded as CSV
- with `~~GTI.i_inspect()`, the rows are numbered (by their place in the data, which stays with
  them as they're sorted and filtered), each column's dtype is under its label (as Polars names it,
  whatever the DataFrame library), missing values are tinted, and the status line says what the
  data is (a Polars DataFrame or LazyFrame, a Pandas DataFrame, a PyArrow Table, a DuckDB relation,
  or an Ibis table) and how many of its rows and columns are left

```{python}
cars = data.pl.gtcars.select(["mfr", "model", "year", "hp", "mpg_c", "msrp"])

GTI(cars, preset="explorer")
```

A preset is only where the table starts: the `i_` methods change it as they'd change any table. Each
sets all of its feature's settings, so `.i_display(wrap=True)` on an explorer lets its text wrap,
but also makes its rows less compact and puts them in the table's own font, unless it's given
`compact=True` and `monospace=True` too; and `.i_inspect(missing=False)` leaves the row numbers,
dtypes and dimensions on. `i_inspect()` and `~~GTI.i_display()` work on their own as well, on any
`GTI` table.

## Exporting the rows

With `~~GTI.i_export()`, an export button in the control bar opens a panel with a button for each
way readers can take the rows away: downloaded as a CSV, TSV or JSON file (`"csv"`, `"tsv"`,
`"json"`), copied (`"clipboard"`), or as code that gets them from the data (`"code"`). Here, filter
the cars to a make or two and sort them, then export what's left; the files are named
`gtcars.csv`, `gtcars.tsv` and `gtcars.json`.

```{python}
(
    GTI(gtcars_pl)
    .tab_header(title="GT Cars: exporting the rows")
    .cols_label(mfr="Make", model="Model", year="Year", hp="HP", trq="Torque", msrp="MSRP")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["year", "hp", "trq"], use_seps=False)
    .fmt_currency(columns="msrp")
    .i_cols_filter(columns="mfr", type="facet")
    .i_export(["csv", "tsv", "json", "clipboard", "code"], filename="gtcars")
)
```

An export has the rows readers see: every row the search and filters keep (on every page, not only
the one shown), in the order shown, with the columns' text as the table shows it (so the Ford GT's
`MSRP` is exported as `$447,000.00`). Each format has them its own way:

- a CSV or TSV file has the column labels as its first row (each after its spanners' labels, as in
  "Revenue – gross"), and with row groups, the group's label as a column before the others; a cell
  a spreadsheet would read as a formula starts with a `'`, so that it's read as text
- a JSON file has an object for each row, with each cell's text under its column's name in the data
  (and the row's group label first, under `"group"`)
- a copy has the rows both as a table, with the cells' styles, for pasting into a document or a
  spreadsheet, and as text, with tabs between the cells
- the code filters and sorts the data (as `df`) as the reader's view does, for Polars, Pandas or
  Narwhals (the data's library, at first); it works on the data's values, so it leaves out the
  search

The formats' buttons are in the order `i_export()` is given them. With `~~GTI.i_selection()`,
readers can export the rows they've selected instead.

## Using the table from Python and in apps

Python can read what readers do with a `GTI` table and change it: in a notebook, with the table as a
widget, in a marimo notebook, and in Shiny, Streamlit, Panel and Solara apps; and a page an app
makes itself, with Flask, Django or FastHTML, can show it. See
[GTI in Python and Apps](26-gti-in-python-and-apps.qmd).
